name: Rain Garden
description: Detroit's first Piet Oudolf design — a 3,803 sq ft (0.25-acre) stormwater management garden that collects and filters runoff from Belle Isle Drive through an innovative inlet and trench drain system. Instead of entering the sewer, stormwater percolates through deep-rooted wetland plants. Created with the Erb Family Foundation and Roy Diblik.

regions.label: Cardinal Flower Zone
regions.notes: Lobelia cardinalis — the most intensely red native wildflower in North America. This westernmost section stays moist from stormwater infiltration, ideal for cardinal flower. Hummingbirds visit regularly from July through September. A captivating sight at close range.

regions.label: Wild Columbine Zone
regions.notes: Aquilegia canadensis — delicate red-and-yellow nodding flowers in April–May. The shallowest, best-drained area of the rain garden suits columbine perfectly. Goes dormant by summer, hidden under taller emerging plants. Self-seeds freely — look for seedlings throughout.

regions.label: Copper Iris Zone
regions.notes: Iris fulva — brick-red to copper-orange flowers in May–June; a color unlike any other iris. The eastern section has the most consistent moisture, suiting this wetland iris. Spreads by rhizomes into dense colonies along the water's edge.

regions.label: Great Blue Lobelia Zone
regions.notes: Lobelia siphilitica — brilliant blue spikes in August–October. The deepest part of the rain garden retains moisture longest — perfect for great blue lobelia. Planted adjacent to cardinal flower to create a blue-and-red combination that is spectacular in late summer.

features.label: Stormwater Inlet
features.description: Stormwater from Belle Isle Drive enters through this inlet and disperses through a trench drain into the garden. The rain garden retains 1,677 cubic feet (12,544 gallons) at capacity — preventing that volume from entering the combined sewer system and protecting nearby Lake Tacoma from nutrient runoff. The deep-rooted plants filter pollutants naturally.

features.label: Hummingbird Nectar Corridor
features.description: Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit the Cardinal Flower (Lobelia cardinalis) here from July through September. The flowers' red color and tubular shape are precisely evolved for hummingbird pollination — bees cannot see red as a distinct color. Watch from the path; hummingbirds are bold and will hover very close.

features.label: Native Wetland Pollinators
features.description: The Rain Garden supports specialist wetland bee species not found elsewhere in the garden, including Hibiscus Sweat Bees (Dieunomia) and Yellow-Banded Bumblebees (Bombus terricola), a species of conservation concern. Great Blue Lobelia's flower tube is specifically sized for bumblebee tongues.
